turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Marcus, quick stuff before Dr. Shah comes in. Pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-four, heart rate seventy-six, and the fingerstick just now was two fourteen. You'd already had coffee, so that isn't a fasting one.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Two fourteen? That's high, I knew it. At home this week I had one-eighty-something fasting, or the napkin said one ninety-two, and the app flashed one seventy-six, and I don't even know if that was before the muffin or—
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): We'll leave the napkin out of the chart. What I do have is Lantus eighteen units at bedtime, and metformin one thousand milligrams twice a day. You still on both?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Eighteen? No, I draw up twenty-four. Every night, twenty-four units. Unless the pen clicks different than the vial did, I switched a while back and nobody—
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hey Marcus, I'm Dr. Shah. I caught the tail end of that. What's been worrying you most?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The sugar, honestly. And my feet. And I keep reading I'm going to go blind, is that, I mean, am I already—
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll talk about your eyes and your feet, I promise. Tell me how the diabetes has actually been day to day.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Messy. I drive a delivery route, like ten hours, and on work days I skip the shot because if I take it I get shaky before I can eat. Nights too, sometimes I skip, no, wait, nights I take it. I'm getting this wrong.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let's untangle it. When you do take the Lantus, what time, and how many units do you dial?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Bedtime. Twenty-four units, I stop the dial at twenty-four. What I skip is the night before a work day, so I won't get shaky on the route. Other nights I take it.
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): I need to flag this. His order and the med list both still say eighteen units of insulin glargine nightly. There's no twenty-four anywhere in the chart.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Then the label at home is wrong, or the chart is. Should I bring the box? And can the wrong dose mess up my kidneys, because that's the part that scares me?

[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bring the box, yes. I'm not going to say your kidneys are damaged off a mismatch like this. High sugars could be the skipped shots, or the dose not matching the order, or meals in the truck, and I won't pick a cause today.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): So not kidney failure? My uncle ended up really sick and I keep thinking that's next, and if you were going to change something I want to know before—
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not kidney failure, not from today. What I was going to do is raise the Lantus by four units and see you back in a month.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Raise it? On twenty-four or on eighteen? That doesn't even—
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're right to stop me. I'm walking that back. No dose change today. Adding insulin when we can't agree on eighteen versus twenty-four is how people get hurt.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. So then what? Do I just keep guessing which number to dial?
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't change the number on your pen until we see the box. No increase. First step is bloodwork, a hemoglobin A1c and a basic metabolic panel, and then we decide the dose.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): A1c is the three-month one, right? Last time they told me seven-something, or maybe it was eight, and I didn't write it down. Was that last winter, or the winter before? I can't tell you.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, the three-month average. We'll get a fresh one and not lean on a result you can't place. How's the metformin going?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): That one I don't skip. One thousand milligrams by mouth, morning and again with supper. Only the insulin is the problem.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other prescriptions besides those two?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, ten milligrams, in the morning, for my blood pressure. Been on it for years. I was taking fish oil too, but I stopped that months ago because of the burps.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Glad you mentioned stopping the fish oil. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I always get scared I'll react to something new, but I've never actually had an allergy.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Tell me about your feet. Any open sores, redness, anything that isn't healing?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No sores. I look, most nights. The toes tingle, pins and needles, worse right after the boots come off. Walking doesn't hurt my calves.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did that tingling start?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't put a date on it. Last winter, or the one before. Maybe when the heater broke, which isn't a real answer. It wasn't like this when I was younger.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Does the tingling mean I'm going to lose a toe? My uncle had type two, like me, and they took his toe. I check for black spots that aren't there.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tingling is a reason to protect the feet, not a toe already lost. And you haven't actually seen black spots?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No black spots. I just picture them. Sorry, I ask a lot of questions when I get scared.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ask all of them. Any surgeries in the past?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Appendix out when I was a kid. Nothing after that. And I never smoked, not once, if you're about to ask.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I was, thank you. What about alcohol, and who's at home with you?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): A beer on Sunday, sometimes two, not every Sunday. I live by myself, so that's the whole story.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): How about the eyes? Any blur, floaters, or a curtain coming across the vision?

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Mornings are fuzzy until I've been up a while. No floaters, and no curtain. Rubbing them doesn't fix it. Is fuzzy the same thing as retinopathy, because I googled it and—
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Google will always show you the worst page. Fuzzy mornings could be the sugar, dry eye, or early diabetic changes in the retina. I am not calling this retinopathy today.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): So you'll still send me somewhere? I can't do dilating drops on a delivery day, I wouldn't be safe to drive. Can it be a Monday? How soon is soon?
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. I'll refer you to ophthalmology for a dilated exam, and they can aim for a Monday. Soon means on the books, not this afternoon.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your feet while you're here.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Skin is intact, no ulcers on the soles or between the toes. Pulses at both ankles are easy to feel. The monofilament feels dulled on both big toes, and it's normal on the balls of the feet.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Dulled, like the nerve is already dead? If I stop skipping shots does it come back? And these shoes I bought online pinch across the toes, do I throw them out?

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I can't promise the feeling comes back, and I didn't say the nerve is dead. Throw out the pinching shoes. Check both feet every day, moisturize, and don't walk barefoot, even at home.

[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the shaky thing, though? When I do take the shot and then can't eat, I get shaky and sweaty, like on the highway. Is that a low? That's the whole reason I skip.

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Shaky and sweaty before you can eat can be a low, yes. I still don't want the whole dose skipped. Carry crackers in the truck, pull over, and check if you feel that way. The unit number stays put until the pen and the chart match.

[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Crackers I can do. Do I have to check before every single meal? Those home numbers, the one-eighty-something, I already told her, I don't trust them, and I don't know if they were even fasting.
[SEG0050] person_1 (NURSE): Still nothing uploaded from his meter. Only today's fingerstick, two fourteen, not fasting.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then we won't pretend we have a home average. Any chest pain lately, or trouble catching your breath?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): The route is brutal, I-40 just sits there every afternoon, and my lower back aches from the seat. That's not what you asked, I know.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): We can come back to the back. Chest and breathing first?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. Breathing is fine. The back is both sides, end of the day, from sitting, not a sharp thing.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Now you've got me thinking the ache is my kidneys. You mentioned kidneys and I can't let it go. Is it?

[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): All-day sitting explains that kind of ache, and I'm not blaming your kidneys for it. The metabolic panel still checks kidney function, because of the diabetes and the lisinopril, not because of the back.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the pee test everybody at work talks about? Do I have to? I drank a ton of water, does that ruin it? If it's bad, is that dialysis?

[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): I was going to skip the urine today and keep this short. Actually, let's add a urine albumin. With the tingling and the sugars all over the place, I'd rather not wait, and extra water won't ruin it.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): So if that albumin is high you have to tell me it isn't dialysis. Please. I need to hear it isn't automatic.

[SEG0060] person_3 (DOCTOR): It isn't automatic, and it isn't today's news. A high albumin can mean early strain on the kidney, and I am not going to tell you that you need dialysis. We don't have the result.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Thank you. I used to walk after dinner and I stopped. Is that part of why the sugar's worse? Should I start again?

[SEG0062] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stopping the walks can nudge the sugar up. It's one more possible piece, not the verdict. If your back allows it, a short walk after meals is worth restarting. Nothing heroic.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Even in the depot parking lot? And if I toss the pinchy shoes, tomorrow I only have the work boots. What if they rub?
[SEG0064] person_3 (DOCTOR): Boots are fine if they aren't rubbing. If the boots break the skin, then we'll do a diabetic shoe referral, but not today.
[SEG0065] person_1 (NURSE): I can draw the A1c, the metabolic panel, and the urine albumin before he goes, if you want all three today.
[SEG0066] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, all three today, thank you. Front desk can book ophthalmology and a return visit in two weeks. Not a month, I don't want to wait that long anymore.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. What if something's scary before that? Do I call, or is it the ER, and what number is the scary one? I don't want to guess and be wrong.

[SEG0068] person_3 (DOCTOR): Call the clinic if you're worried but still okay. If you're confused, vomiting and can't keep fluids down, or the meter reads over four hundred and won't come down, go to the ER. Otherwise I'll see you in two weeks, and bring the Lantus box.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

bad.reason: Fingerstick was completed, but transcript doesn't say nurse requested it.
Carry crackers and pull over/check if shaky supported; doctor says he still doesn't want whole dose skipped, not absolute 'do not skip'.
